intro: Pharmacists build complex problem solving, judgment and service skills that research, teaching and health management roles depend on. Of the 25 careers below, Clinical Research Coordinators match pharmacists most closely at 73%, followed by Medical Dosimetrists at 70%.
why_it_works: Pharmacy combines precise science with fast, careful decisions and steady contact with patients and doctors. O*NET rates complex problem solving, judgment and time management at 3.88 out of 5 for pharmacists, the same strengths that clinical research and health management roles ask for. Clinical trials rely on the drug knowledge and attention to detail you use every shift. Teaching and counseling roles build on the patient education you already do. Expect to add skills like programming and budgeting.
tips: Be realistic about pay: pharmacists earn a high median, so only 4 of the 25 matches pay more.
Look at industry roles in clinical trials, drug safety and regulatory affairs, where a pharmacy degree is a strong credential.
Learn one data tool, since programming is the top skill gap across the closest matches.

faq.q: What can pharmacists do besides working in a pharmacy?
faq.a: The closest matches are Clinical Research Coordinators (73%), Medical Dosimetrists (70%) and Health Specialties Teachers, Postsecondary (68%), based on O*NET 31.0. Genetic Counselors (68%) and Clinical Data Managers (66%) are also close and use your science background away from the counter.

faq.q: Which careers pay more than pharmacy?
faq.a: Only 4 of the 25 matches pay more than the $140,910 median for pharmacists in BLS May 2025 data. Industrial-Organizational Psychologists earn $193,950 (+38%), Natural Sciences Managers earn $167,220 (+19%) and Medical Dosimetrists earn $147,470 (+5%). Many other moves trade some pay for better hours.

faq.q: Do pharmacists need another degree to change careers?
faq.a: Not for any option on this page: all 25 matches usually need no more education than a Pharm.D., based on O*NET Job Zones. Some roles still ask for a certification, such as medical dosimetry, where a professional certification is often expected.

faq.q: What skills should pharmacists build for a new career?
faq.a: Across the top 10 matches, the skills that most often need work are programming, operation and control, instructing and managing financial resources. Your strongest skills, such as complex problem solving at 3.88 out of 5, already match what research and management roles need.
